title: India's Monsoon Is 43% Below Normal. The Government Just Drew Up Emergency Plans for 315 Districts.
excerpt: El Niño is forecast to deliver the weakest rains in 11 years. Farmers are already switching crops, Mumbai is rationing water, and food-price inflation is the elephant in every policy room.
body:
India's farm minister has acknowledged what satellite imagery and empty fields have been saying for weeks: the monsoon is failing. On Tuesday, Shivraj Singh Chouhan chaired an emergency meeting with state agriculture ministers, weather officials and scientists, and confirmed that the government has prepared contingency plans for more than 315 districts — nearly half the country — to cope with a rainfall deficit that currently stands at 43% below the long-period average.

The India Meteorological Department has forecast that this year's southwest monsoon will deliver just 90% of normal rainfall, the lowest in 11 years. The culprit is a strengthening El Niño, the Pacific Ocean warming pattern that disrupts India's seasonal rain machine. June, typically the month when the monsoon surges across the subcontinent, has been particularly grim: the first three weeks recorded a 42% deficit, and the IMD expects weak rains to persist through at least July 2.

## 111 Districts on High Alert

Of the 315 districts in the government's contingency framework, 111 have been classified as high priority — areas where less than a quarter of farmland has access to irrigation. Another 76 are medium priority. For these regions, a weak monsoon is not an inconvenience; it is an existential threat to the agricultural cycle that sustains roughly half of India's 1.4 billion people.

The government has asked states to nudge farmers toward short-duration, water-efficient crops: pulses, millets and oilseeds instead of water-hungry rice and sugarcane. States have been directed to repair ponds, check dams and water-harvesting structures ahead of whatever rains do arrive. In Maharashtra's sugar belt, farmers are already pivoting. Sambhaji Patil, who farms in Sangli district, told Reuters he had planned to plant cane but switched to soybeans after hearing forecasts. Nursery operators report a sharp drop in demand for cane seedlings.

## Mumbai Rations, Reservoirs Drop

The monsoon's advance across western India stalled for two weeks in mid-June, leaving Mumbai — a city of 21 million — waiting. Water supplies to construction sites have been cut, and industrial usage has been reduced by 20% as reservoir levels decline. The rains finally pushed into southern Maharashtra late last week, and the IMD now says Mumbai will likely see monsoon rains imminently. But the late start has left a deficit that may take weeks to recover, if it recovers at all.

The stall was caused by western disturbances — weather systems from the Mediterranean that brought unseasonal rain and snow to northern India and blocked the monsoon's northward advance. The monsoon has now moved into parts of Maharashtra, Telangana, Chhattisgarh and Karnataka, but its progress remains sluggish.

## The Inflation Risk

The economic stakes are enormous. The monsoon delivers about 70% of India's annual rainfall and directly influences the kharif (summer) sowing season, when farmers plant rice, corn, cotton, soybeans and sugarcane. A weak monsoon can slash crop yields, drag down rural incomes and push up food prices — a chain reaction that feeds into inflation.

India's retail inflation stood at 3.48% in April, driven partly by higher food prices. Economists warn that a deficient monsoon, particularly in the crucial July-August window, could push inflation toward 5.5%. "A deficient monsoon can add to the pressure and push up inflation closer to an average of 5.5% if food inflation spikes," said Gaura Sengupta, chief economist at IDFC First Bank.

The Reserve Bank of India has so far resisted rate hikes, with Governor Sanjay Malhotra saying it is premature to discuss tightening when inflation remains below the central bank's 4% target. But a prolonged rain deficit would force a rethink.

## Ample Stocks, But Prices Will Still Bite

India does have a buffer. Government warehouses hold ample stocks of rice and wheat, enough to meet domestic demand even if the kharif harvest falls short. But stock levels and retail prices are different animals. Higher procurement costs, transport disruptions and speculative hoarding can push up prices at the mandi even when aggregate supply is adequate.

The sugar sector is already feeling the squeeze. India was expected to produce 30.95 million tonnes this season, but output forecasts have been revised down to 27.9 million tonnes — below annual consumption of 28.5 million tonnes. Mill inventories at the start of the new season in October are projected to hit a three-decade low of 3.5 million tonnes.

Meanwhile, India's ethanol-blending programme is competing for the same cane. The government is pushing for higher ethanol blending with petrol and wider adoption of flex-fuel vehicles to cut dependence on imported crude. Ethanol demand could more than double to 30 billion litres by 2039-40 from the current 12-13 billion litres. Cane supply is being pulled in two directions, and the monsoon has just made both pulls tighter.

## What NRIs Should Watch

For the diaspora, the monsoon is not abstract. Millions of NRI families send remittances to relatives in rural India — money that often supplements farm income. A weak monsoon means lower yields, lower prices at the farm gate, and a heavier reliance on those remittances. Food prices at the local market will also rise, eating into the purchasing power of the rupees being sent home.

The broader economic impact matters too. Rural consumption drives roughly 35-40% of India's consumer spending. A hit to farm incomes ripples through auto sales, FMCG volumes and discretionary spending. Companies that depend on rural India — from two-wheeler makers to consumer-goods giants — have already flagged caution in recent earnings calls.

The next four weeks will be decisive. If July rains pick up, the deficit can narrow and the kharif season can still be salvaged. If El Niño strengthens as forecast, India will be managing a full agricultural emergency by August.
